hints: Look at Fig. 1.1 from left to right - compare the depth of the U-shaped loop in P, Q and R with the label under each collecting duct.
walkthrough:
Compare the three diagrams side by side**
You can see P has a very short loop that barely goes into the medulla, Q has a medium-length loop, and R has a very long loop that goes deep down. All are drawn to the same scale, so this difference is real.

Match loop length to urine label**
P with the shortest loop makes urine with high water potential, meaning dilute urine with lots of water left in it. Q makes urine with low water potential and R with the longest loop makes urine with very low water potential, meaning very concentrated urine with little water left.
Final answer: The longer the loop of Henle, the lower the water potential of the urine.

hints: Think about where a camel lives and how often it can drink - what is the biggest challenge for water balance there?
Link very low water potential urine to water loss - what does losing less water in urine allow the camel to do?
walkthrough:
Remember the camel habitat**
Camels live in hot deserts where drinking water is scarce and water is easily lost by sweating and breathing. Survival depends on keeping as much water inside the body as possible.

Link concentrated urine to conservation**
Urine with very low water potential is very concentrated - it contains a lot of solute in very little water. That means most of the water filtered into the nephron has been reabsorbed back into the blood instead of being lost. This conserves body water, which is vital in a dry environment.
Final answer: Camel lives in a dry / desert environment with little water; produces small volume of highly concentrated urine to conserve water / minimise water loss.

hints: Start with what selective reabsorption does in the PCT - which useful substances must be moved out of the tubule fluid and back to blood?
For microvilli, think about the shape of the cell surface - how does folding the membrane change the area available for carriers and channels?
For many mitochondria, ask what process in the PCT needs a constant supply of ATP - how are $Na^{+}$ ions moved?
Remember that $Na^{+}$ pumping by $Na^{+}$/$K^{+}$ pumps sets up gradients for co-transport of glucose and amino acids - why would stopping ATP supply stop all of this?
For tight junctions, picture the gaps between neighbouring cells - what would happen if tubule fluid could simply leak between cells straight into tissue fluid?
Link tight junctions to control - why must everything pass through the cell membranes rather than around the cells?
walkthrough:
Recall the job of the PCT**
In the proximal convoluted tubule all glucose and amino acids, most $Na^{+}$ ions and water are reabsorbed from filtrate back into blood. This is selective - useful substances are taken back, while urea and excess ions are left to be excreted. The cells need adaptations for fast, controlled uptake.

Microvilli - more membrane for uptake**
Microvilli are tiny finger-like folds of the apical membrane facing the tubule lumen, forming a brush border. They greatly increase surface area, so there is much more membrane packed with carrier proteins and channels for $Na^{+}$, glucose and amino acids. More area means faster absorption by facilitated diffusion and co-transport.

Many mitochondria - ATP for active transport**
Pumping $Na^{+}$ out of the cell into tissue fluid and $K^{+}$ in is done by $Na^{+}$/$K^{+}$ pumps in the basal membrane. This is active transport against concentration gradients and needs ATP from aerobic respiration. Many mitochondria supply that ATP. The $Na^{+}$ gradient created then drives uptake of glucose and amino acids with $Na^{+}$ by co-transport.

Tight junctions - forcing a controlled route**
Tight junctions seal neighbouring PCT cells together. They prevent tubule fluid leaking between cells directly into blood. This means every substance must go through the cell surface membranes where carriers and pumps can select what is reabsorbed and what stays in the tubule. That is what makes reabsorption selective and prevents back-leak.

Final answer: Microvilli: provide large surface area for absorption of $Na^{+}$, glucose and amino acids. Many mitochondria: provide ATP for $Na^{+}$/$K^{+}$ pumps / active transport of $Na^{+}$ and $K^{+}$. Tight junctions: hold adjacent cells together so fluid cannot pass between cells and substances must pass through cells, allowing selective control.
